1.1: 1.1 Argument. The apostle James instructs the holy clergy about the cultivation of the heavenly precepts, and the rule of Catholic observance, and the majesty of unconquered patience, and the revelation of many things, and the commissioning of teachers. James. He undertook the care and governance of the Church of Jerusalem, after the apostles were sent out to preach. To the twelve tribes. To have special concern for these belonged to the twelve apostles, who performed the embassy for the Lord among the circumcision. Hence Paul also says: James, and Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave their right hands, etc. Therefore he writes especially to them, and because he himself had been appointed bishop over them by the other apostles.
1.2: 1.2 All joy. Do not be indignant if the wicked flourish in the world while you suffer, because it is not the mark of Christian truth to be exalted in temporal things, but rather to be cast down. The wicked have nothing in heaven; you have nothing in the world. In the hope of that good toward which you are striving, you ought to rejoice in whatever happens on the way. When you fall into temptations. He begins with the external temptations, addressing those more perfect.
1.3: 1.3 The trial of your faith, etc. BEDE. The same sentence, but in reversed order, is read in Paul, etc., down to by which faith is proved perfect.
1.6: 1.6 But he who doubts. He who, weighed down by the consciousness of sin, doubts about the heavenly rewards, when the wind of temptations comes upon him, easily abandons the state of faith, and according to the will of the tempter is carried along by the blast of the wind through various errors of vices.
1.10: 1.10 But the rich man. He calls rich the one who places all his hope in riches; it is not harmful to have riches, but to love them. But let the rich man glory. Ironically. As if to say: He ought not to glory in his own glory, by which he is proud and oppresses others, because it must come to an end and be humbled in hell. Or, Let him glory in his humility, that is, not in pride, but let him humble himself by serving others out of his riches. For as the flower of the grass. The just man flourishes like the palm tree, the unjust like grass: because the former remains, the latter quickly passes away. The flower of the just man is the hope that awaits fruit, the root of the just man is charity, which remains immovable; the root of the wicked is cupidity, their flower the delight in temporal things.
1.11: 1.11 The rich man in his ways. The ways of the rich man are temporal things, by which he seeks to be made happy, and which will quickly be destroyed. The heat of the sun is the coming of the severe Judge: either unforeseen in the death of each person, or in the judgment in common. In which the just man will remain like a fruitful tree.
1.12: 1.12 Blessed is the man. Because it is difficult to exhort to contempt of the world, he adds about the greatness of the reward: Blessed is the man, etc. You ought to suffer not only blows and prisons, but also the loss of temporal goods, which are cheap and transitory, and those who love them are to be punished.
1.13: 1.13 Let no one, when he is tempted. BEDE. Thus far about external temptations; now, etc., down to and that man sins as if by necessity. That he is tempted by God. God sends external temptation for the testing of his own; but God does not send the internal temptation by which theft, adultery, murder are often conceived.
1.14: 1.14 Each one is tempted. There are two kinds of temptations: one that tests, as God tempted Abraham. The other that deceives, as in the saying that God tempts no one. When we build upon the foundation wood, hay, stubble, the devil sets fire on top. Let us build gold, silver, precious stones: and he will not dare to tempt; yet he does not desist altogether, but sits in hiding places to kill the innocent. Brings forth death. Just as the one who is tempted and overcomes receives the rewards of life, so the one who is enticed by his desires and overcome deservedly incurs the ruin of death.
1.17: 1.17 Every gift, etc. BEDE. After he taught that vices are not from God to us, but from ourselves, etc., down to can be understood as the perfect gift. Nor shadow of change. No shadow keeps his light from sending any evils. The goods of light are always in God, but his gifts in us are sometimes such that sins coming upon them overshadow them.
1.18: 1.18 Willingly. Every good is from God, and you did not come to this by your merits, but by the grace alone of the divine will. That we might be a beginning, etc. Through this begetting let us not suppose that we are what he himself is, but that by adoption he has granted us a certain primacy among creatures. Hence another translator: That we might be the firstfruits of his creatures.
1.19: 1.19 Slow to anger. Let no one be angry rashly and without cause, whether against subjects who sin, or against any brothers, or against the prosperity of the wicked, because the maturity of wisdom is perceived only with a tranquil mind. And he who judges in anger, even if he judges justice, still cannot imitate the justice of the divine examination, in which no disturbance falls.
1.21: 1.21 Wherefore casting aside, etc. He admonished them to seek doctrine, and, to receive it and be able to progress in it, he now exhorts them to cleanness of body and soul. For he who does not turn away from evil cannot do good. The implanted word. The word which by preaching we place in your hearts, or the word which was implanted and sown in the day of redemption, when God begot you; now receive it more perfectly, and fulfil in works what you hold in mystery.
1.23: 1.23 Considering his face. He who sets himself to consider in the Scriptures, as in a mirror, the face of his birth, how man is born, how frail, and what he will become, of how short a life, in how many miseries placed, conceives great compunction and the will to repent; but soon, seduced by some temptation, he forgets the compunction and returns to sins. With this inconstancy he compares the one who gladly hears the word and neglects to fulfil it. And there is a likeness between the one who of his own accord, without a teacher, applied himself to the Scriptures, and the one who hears the Scriptures from another, since neither has fulfilled them. A child when born cries, by which the sorrow of the soul is indicated, and that it enters life into the miseries of the flesh; this sorrow it afterwards forgets, the soul being accustomed to the allurements of the flesh.
1.26: 1.26 Not bridling his tongue, etc. AUGUSTINE, Sermon 3 to the brothers in the desert. What else is talkativeness? etc., down to and you should attend diligently: He who does not bridle his tongue, this man's religion is vain, etc.
1.27: 1.27 And to keep oneself unspotted from this world. By world he means the cosmos, or all things that are in the world, such as the concupiscence of the flesh, and of the eyes, and the pride of life.
2.1: 2.1 Do not. As if he says: The Lord does not invite the rich to faith and despise the poor, but he chose the poor in this world, and endowed them with faith. The world casts out the poor and honors the rich; the faith of Christ teaches the opposite, that all the glory of the rich is like the flower of grass, while mercy toward the poor flowers for ever. Of the Lord of glory. He names the Lord of glory so that his commands may be obeyed, he who rewards with everlasting glory what is given to the poor out of love for him.
2.5: 2.5 Hear. BEDE. Attend more carefully, because he did not make illustrious and noble those who are richer in the world, etc., down to but he has made these illustrious and noble through the expectation of the kingdom to come. Has not God. BEDE. God chose the poor, who says elsewhere: Do not be afraid, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom. He also chose poor parents, by whose service he was nourished.
2.6: 2.6 Do not the rich. He shows more openly whom he meant above by the rich, namely those who prefer riches to Christ, and who, being themselves strangers to the faith, oppress by their power those who believe, and drag them to the courts of the more powerful. And this is another reason why they are not to be chosen, that they bring evils upon the faithful.
2.7: 2.7 They blaspheme. In the times of the apostles, many of the Gentiles and Jews, especially the wealthier, are found to have done these things.
2.8: 2.8 If however you fulfil the law. Because he had spoken harshly and with contempt of the rich, and in a certain way contrary to the divine law, which commands that all be loved, lest the rich be thought to be altogether despised, he adds: as if he says, for the aforesaid reasons they are not to be chosen, but if you fulfil this law which says: You shall love your neighbor (Matthew 22), you do well; because, although the rich are not to be chosen on account of riches, they are nevertheless not to be loved less for God's sake. Royal. That is, excellent, or because it is common to all and embraces all. Or the law which says: Do not shame the person of the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful (Leviticus 19), and elsewhere: There shall be no distinction of persons: you shall hear the small as well as the great, because the judgment is God's (Deuteronomy 1).
2.10: 2.10 But whoever. Lest they think it a contemptible sin to transgress the law in this one matter, he adds: But whoever, etc. Yet offends in one point, he is become guilty of all. Truly he who offends in one point is a transgressor of the whole law, because he who sins acts against the author of the law, whom he neglects in his law, and against charity, which is the cause and mother of the whole law. Let us see this statement by a comparison: if someone offended me, he would offend all my brothers and friends in me, and in a certain way would sin against all. So he who neglects one commandment renders useless to himself the rest, which seemed to help when they were fulfilled.
2.12: 2.12 So speak. BEDE. Since it is wrong for a rich man to be chosen on account of riches, etc., down to which calls the willing to repentance and forgives sins. As if he said: Speak well, and do well: for if you neglect this, you will be condemned more severely than those who lived in the time of Moses, because to whom more is entrusted, more is required of him. The more a person obtains greater mercy from the Lord, the more unjustly he denies mercy to a needy neighbor, and the more justly he pays the penalties of impiety.
2.13: 2.13 But mercy exalts itself. BEDE. As in the judgment he will grieve who did not show mercy, so he who did will exult and rejoice, rewarded.
2.14: 2.14 What shall it profit, etc. The same. Here he disputes more broadly about the works of mercy, so as to console those whom he had terrified by the preceding statement, teaching by what remedies daily sins are expiated, without which life is not lived. Lest those who offend not in one point only, but in many, be found guilty of all in the judgment.
2.18: 2.18 But someone will say. You ought to be spurred to work well not only for the reasons already stated, but also so that you may not suffer reproach from others, because someone, taking confidence from his own works, in order to show that faith alone is of no avail, will say in reproach: You have faith, etc.
2.19: 2.19 You believe, etc. He proved that those who have no works do not have true faith; now he reveals what kind of faith they have, lest they make much of such a faith. The devils also believe, and tremble. BEDE. It is written, etc., down to are to be considered slower and more headstrong than the devils.
2.20: 2.20 But will you know, O vain man? BEDE. Having proved that faith without works is dead, etc., down to let them imitate in temptation and in action.
2.21: 2.21 Abraham our father, etc. The same. That Abraham is said to have been justified by faith without works, etc., down to is set forth as an example concerning both. Offering up his son Isaac upon the altar? A great temptation, when he was commanded to kill his son; a great faith, when he believed that he could receive seed even from one dead; a great work, when he did not hesitate to offer his most beloved.
2.22: 2.22 You see that faith cooperated with his works, and by works, etc. Because he offered him in whom he had received the promise, the great power of faith appears: for even if he offered him, he believed the promise would be fulfilled, since he believed God able even to raise the dead. In like manner also Rahab the harlot. BEDE. Lest they object that they could not imitate the works of so great a father, etc., down to and counted in the generations of the Savior.
3.1: 3.1 Be not. As I admonished you to do works, so I admonish you to avoid foolish teaching. Be not many. There were many in the times of the apostles who, coming down from Judea to Antioch, not well instructed in the law of faith, taught that believers from the Gentiles must be circumcised, and introduced other errors, which caused the true preachers no small labor of controversy. He therefore removes these from the office of the word, lest they hinder the true preachers. The greater. BEDE. He who, unlearned, usurps the office of teaching, and does not announce Christ sincerely, deserves a greater condemnation than if he perished alone by his own crime; just as, on the contrary, he who ministers well acquires for himself a good rank.
3.2: 3.2 In many things. It is truly dangerous to want to preside over the rest, because not only you who are less learned, but all of us preachers, even the greater, offend in many things, some by teaching badly, others by living badly, and others in other ways. The blessed Apostle counts himself with them, that he may rebuke more freely. The just man offends in one way, the wicked in another; the just man offends through the frailty of the flesh, and does not cease to be just; hence Solomon: The just man shall fall seven times a day and shall rise again; as the offense is daily, so the remedy of prayers and good works is daily, but the impious fall into evil. If any man. He wishes to show the inevitable offense of speech, to deter the inexperienced, lest they desire prelacy: for he who desires to preside must be more perfect than others, lest he offend when he ought to profit; but the inexperienced cannot but offend in preaching. Offends not in word. BEDE. That is, in that offense of which human frailty can steer clear. Such as a word of deceit, of detraction, of pride, of boasting, and also of idle and superfluous speech; this is a perfect man.
3.3: 3.3 For if we put bits into the mouths of horses. BEDE. Much more ought we to put them into our own mouths. Some books have: As bits into the mouths of horses, and it is joined thus to what follows: As we put bits into the mouths of horses, so also the tongue is indeed a little member, and boasts great things.
3.5: 3.5 And boasts great things. The same. It exalts rewards, if the impulse of the one directing governs it well; if badly, it exalts great destruction for himself and his own, hence Solomon: Death and life are in the power of the tongue (Proverbs 18). It exalts life if it teaches the Church well; death if badly. For he argues against those who, destitute of both life and knowledge, presumed to teach. The tongue therefore exalts great things when, despising the words and senses of the rest, it singularly boasts itself wise and eloquent. Against this: Do not multiply speaking lofty things, boasting. Behold how great a fire. So also the incontinent tongue causes a great store of good works to perish, and thus, since it is almost impossible to avoid the sin of the tongue even for the perfect, not just anyone ought to seek the office of teacher.
3.6: 3.6 A world of iniquity. He says world, because through it almost all crimes are either devised, such as robberies and rapes; or perpetrated, such as perjuries and false testimonies; or defended, as when any impure person, in excusing the crime he committed, pretends a good that he did not do. Which defiles the whole body. And because the tongue is such, it defiles the whole body, and causes it to be reckoned unclean in the sight of God, and therefore it is a grave matter to undertake the office of teaching: because it is set among our members, it is one of our members, far too near to us. It inflames the wheel, etc. BEDE. It contaminates the whole course of temporal life, etc., down to compels to carry into effect through the other members.
3.7: 3.7 For every nature of beasts, etc. The same. We read in Pliny that a most savage asp in Egypt was tamed by a certain head of a household, and used to come out of its cave daily and receive its ration from his table. We read in Marcellinus of a tigress made tame, sent from India to the prince Anastasius.
3.10: 3.10 Out of the same mouth proceeds. Others, seeing what we do, are led by our example to bless and curse likewise. It ought not. Truly it ought not that with the same mouth we bless the head and curse the members, because the sweetness of blessing is consumed by the bitterness of cursing.
3.11: 3.11 Does a fountain? The preacher must sometimes use bitter preaching, by drawing away, by rebuking. It is rather difficult for him to do both with different words tending to the same end.
3.12: 3.12 Can a fig tree, brethren? It cannot be that a teacher be a fig tree with the sweetness of the beatitude to which he exhorts, and use sweet words, and be a vine making men forget all temporal things, for which it is necessary to use harsh words: this therefore is difficult. Thus neither can salt water make sweet water, that is, a preacher who bites sharply at the morals of others cannot in the same teaching be sweet to the same people.
3.13: 3.13 Who is wise and instructed among you? Having refuted those who have neither holiness of life nor restraint of the tongue, he admonishes those who seemed to themselves wise, or even were, to show wisdom rather by living with discipline than by teaching others, because he who is more inclined to teaching than to doing sometimes incurs boasting, or contention, or envy against other teachers, and many other evils.
